cultivar: Fenghuang Shui Xian, Zhi Lan Xiang strain
processing: Sun-withered, shaken through the night to a medium-light oxidation, fixed, rolled into long strips and charcoal roasted light to medium; high-mountain lots are roasted gently to protect the orchid aroma.
harvest_season: Spring, April into early May on the higher slopes; a mid-season strain, and the spring picking is the one that matters.
appearance_dry: Long, slightly curved olive-brown strips with a sharp, clean floral smell.
appearance_wet: Long, thick yellow-green leaves with red edges.
taste_profile: A high, clean orchid aroma with a hint of citrus peel, a medium body with a honeyed sweetness, and a long, cooling finish that keeps the floral note going after the sip.

brewing.notes: Boiling water, thin gaiwan, flash steeps. Serve in small, thin cups and smell them when empty; Zhi Lan Xiang leaves a strong orchid note on the porcelain. Over-steeping makes it sharp.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, spring tea on sale from around June after a light roast, or from autumn for medium roasts and Wudong lots. Best within one to two years for the light roasts; medium-roasted high-mountain tea keeps three years or more sealed and dry.
description:
Zhi Lan Xiang, orchid fragrance, is the dancong for people who want the floral side of Phoenix tea without sweetness turning it soft: a high, clean orchid aroma with a citrus edge and a long cool finish. Among the ten classic aroma types it is often thought of as the elegant one.

The zhi lan of the name is a classical phrase for fragrant plants, usually read as orchid. The name covers several lines rather than a single tree, among them Zhu Ye Zhi Lan Xiang and Li Xia Zhi Lan, and the type is grown across the Fenghuang range at many elevations and prices.

It is made in the standard dancong way, sun-withered, shaken overnight, rolled into strips and charcoal roasted, with makers tending toward a lighter roast than they would give Mi Lan Xiang so the aroma stays bright. In the cup it opens with orchid and a hint of citrus peel, has a honeyed middle and a medium body, and finishes cool and long; the floral note hangs in the mouth and on the empty cup.

It rewards careful brewing more than most: lots of leaf in a thin gaiwan, boiling water, instant pours, and small cups. Steeped too long it loses its poise and goes sharp. Eight infusions is normal, and the fourth and fifth are usually the best balance of aroma and body.

Sold by year with the elevation and village stated by any serious seller, it is best within a year or two for lighter roasts. If you like it, the next steps are Yu Lan Xiang for a softer, magnolia-like floral, and a Wudong lao cong Zhi Lan Xiang to taste what old trees add underneath the flowers.
sources_note: Named single trees of this type on Wudong are often cited in Chaozhou sources; none are named here to avoid unverifiable claims.
history:
Zhi Lan Xiang is one of the ten aroma types of Phoenix dancong, named for its orchid-like scent. Like other aroma names it covers more than one tree, with names such as Zhu Ye Zhi Lan Xiang and Li Xia Zhi Lan pointing to separate lines.

Little is documented about its origin or who first singled it out.
